title: End-of-lesson expressions
prompt: Match the English expressions with their English definitions.

We've run out of time.
An explanation that no time remains.
Stop now.
A direct command to stop immediately.
We'll have to stop here.
A statement that the class must pause at the present point.

Just a second.

One more thing before you go.
An introduction to a final announcement before pupils leave.

prompt: The teacher sees that the lesson-ending bell has just sounded and explicitly points it out to the class.
explanation: “There’s the bell” draws attention to a bell that has just sounded. “The bell hasn’t gone yet” says the opposite; “We’ve run out of time” mentions time rather than the sound; the holiday wish is unrelated.

prompt: The teacher wants to warn pupils that the lesson will end soon, but it is not time to stop yet.
explanation: “It’s almost time to stop” signals that the ending is approaching. “It’s time to finish now” and “Stop now” require an immediate ending; “We’ve run out of time” says no time remains.

prompt: The teacher needs to end the current activity immediately. Choose the short, direct command.
options: One minute to finish that activity.
We seem to have finished early.
explanation: “Stop now” is a direct instruction to end the activity immediately. The one-minute announcement allows more work; finishing early comments on timing; “Have you finished?” asks a question rather than giving a command.

prompt: Pupils have finished writing. The teacher asks them to put their textbooks inside their bags.
options: Take a worksheet as you leave.
explanation: “Pack up your books” asks pupils to put books away. Collecting work involves submitted papers; taking a worksheet means receiving a handout; checking desk tidiness does not instruct pupils to pack books.

prompt: Before collecting notebooks, the teacher asks whether pupils have completed the assigned work.
options: Prepare the next chapter for Tuesday.
explanation: “Have you finished?” checks task completion. “Collect your work” asks for papers, “Are your desks tidy?” checks cleanliness, and preparing the next chapter assigns future work.

prompt: The pupils should submit completed papers to the teacher, rather than put away their books.
options: Take a worksheet as you leave.
explanation: “Collect your work, please” asks for completed work to be handed in or gathered. Packing books, taking a worksheet, and checking desk tidiness are different classroom actions.

prompt: Only one minute remains for the task. The teacher announces exactly that amount of time.
options: We still have a couple of minutes left.
One minute to finish that activity.
There are still three minutes to go.
explanation: “One minute to finish that activity” gives exactly one minute. “A couple of minutes” suggests approximately two; “three minutes” specifies three; “almost time” gives no exact amount.

prompt: Some pupils want to leave, but the bell has not sounded yet. The teacher explains why they must stay.
options: We seem to have finished early.
There are still three minutes to go.
explanation: “The bell hasn’t gone yet” explicitly explains that dismissal is premature. “There’s the bell” states the opposite; finishing early describes progress; three minutes remaining gives a duration, not the stated reason.

prompt: The lesson ends at 10:10, not at 10:00. The teacher names the exact ending time.
options: We'll finish this exercise next lesson.
There are still three minutes to go.
We still have a couple of minutes left.
The lesson doesn't finish till ten past.
explanation: “The lesson doesn’t finish till ten past” names the ending as ten minutes past the hour. The alternatives refer to a later exercise or vague amounts of time, not that scheduled end.

prompt: The class completed all planned activities ahead of schedule. The teacher comments on this unexpectedly early finish.
options: We've run out of time, so we'll continue next lesson.
We seem to have finished early.
explanation: “We seem to have finished early” describes unexpectedly completing the planned work ahead of schedule. The other options describe insufficient time or an immediate ending, not early completion.

prompt: The teacher has a final announcement to make before dismissing pupils, rather than asking them merely to wait.
options: One more thing before you go.
explanation: “One more thing before you go” introduces a final announcement. “Just a moment”, “Hang on a moment”, and “Just a sec” merely ask pupils to wait and do not announce extra information.

prompt: The teacher wants to remind pupils not to forget the homework already assigned.
options: This is your homework for tonight.
What do you have to do before the next lesson?
explanation: “Remember your homework” reminds pupils about work already set. “This is your homework” introduces an assignment; “There is no homework” cancels it; the question asks pupils to recall the task themselves.

prompt: The teacher wants pupils to pick up a printed worksheet on their way out.
options: Prepare the next chapter for Tuesday.
Take a worksheet as you leave.
explanation: “Take a worksheet as you leave” instructs pupils to pick up a handout on departure. The alternatives concern preparing a chapter, submitting completed work, or finishing an exercise.

prompt: To check whether pupils remember their assignment for the next lesson, the teacher asks them to say what they must do.
options: Prepare the next chapter for Tuesday.
This is your homework for tonight.
What do you have to do before the next lesson?
explanation: “What do you have to do before the next lesson?” asks pupils to state their assignment. The alternatives either give an instruction or announce/remind pupils about homework without checking their recall.

prompt: The teacher assigns a specific reading preparation deadline: the new chapter must be ready by Tuesday.
options: Prepare the next chapter for Tuesday.
The next class starts at 7 o'clock.
This is your homework for tonight.
explanation: “Prepare the next chapter for Tuesday” sets both the required preparation and its Tuesday deadline. The other options describe class time, a generic exercise, or homework without the specified chapter and deadline.

prompt: The teacher explicitly tells the class that they have no assignment to complete this evening.
options: This is your homework for tonight.
explanation: “There is no homework tonight” explicitly says no task is assigned for the evening. The other options assign, mention, or remind pupils of work instead.

prompt: The teacher plans to finish the same unfinished exercise during the next lesson, not the whole chapter.
options: We'll do some more practice of this in the next class.
We'll do the rest of this chapter next time.
We'll continue this chapter next Monday.
We'll finish this exercise next lesson.
explanation: “We’ll finish this exercise next lesson” promises to complete the unfinished exercise. The other options refer to practice in general or continuing a chapter rather than finishing this particular exercise.

prompt: The teacher announces that the following class starts at 7:00.
options: We'll finish this exercise next lesson.
The next class starts at 7 o'clock.
We'll continue this chapter next Monday.
explanation: “The next class starts at 7 o’clock” states the exact starting time. The others refer to finishing an exercise, a different time of day, or continuing a chapter.

prompt: After this lesson, pupils will practise the same material more in the following class.
options: We'll do some more practice of this in the next class.
We'll do the rest of this chapter next time.
We've run out of time, so we'll continue next lesson.
We'll finish this exercise next lesson.
explanation: “We’ll do some more practice of this in the next class” promises additional practice on the same material. The others concern a chapter, general continuation after running out of time, or completing one exercise.

prompt: The teacher says goodbye and specifies that they will meet again on Thursday next week.
explanation: “See you again next Thursday” names the next meeting as Thursday of the following week. “Tomorrow afternoon” gives a different time; “Goodbye, everyone” has no date; the holiday wish has a different function.

prompt: Pupils must first stand in a line and then wait there until the bell rings.
options: Try not to make any noise as you leave.
Form a queue and wait for the bell.
explanation: “Form a queue and wait for the bell” includes both lining up and waiting until the bell. “Get into a queue” includes only the first action; the other options concern quiet departure or tidying up.
